disease.name: Coronary Artery Disease
disease.scientific_name: Coronary Heart Disease / Ischemic Heart Disease

overview.description: Coronary Artery Disease (CAD) is a condition where the major blood vessels supplying the heart (coronary arteries) become narrowed or blocked by plaque buildup (atherosclerosis). This reduces blood flow to the heart muscle, leading to chest pain (angina), shortness of breath, or heart attack (myocardial infarction). It is the most common form of heart disease.
overview.prevalence: Affects over 244 million people worldwide; leading cause of death globally.
overview.age_group: Primarily middle-aged and older adults (risk increases significantly after age 45 in men and 55 in women)

types.name: Stable Angina
types.description: Predictable chest pain triggered by exertion or stress, relieved by rest or nitroglycerin.
types.common_in: Patients with moderate coronary artery narrowing

types.name: Unstable Angina
types.description: Unpredictable chest pain occurring at rest or with minimal exertion; precursor to heart attack.
types.common_in: Patients at high risk of acute coronary syndrome

types.name: Microvascular Coronary Disease (INOCA)
types.description: Angina due to dysfunction in small heart vessels without major artery blockages.
types.common_in: Women and patients without classic obstructive CAD

types.name: Silent Ischemia
types.description: Reduced blood flow to heart without noticeable symptoms.

types.name: Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS)
types.description: Includes unstable angina, NSTEMI, and STEMI heart attacks.

severity_levels.name: Asymptomatic / Mild
severity_levels.frequency: Minimal or no symptoms; early plaque buildup
severity_levels.impact: Managed primarily with lifestyle changes and risk factor control

severity_levels.name: Moderate (Stable Angina)
severity_levels.impact: Requires medications; some limitation in physical activity

severity_levels.name: Severe / Unstable
severity_levels.frequency: Symptoms at rest or minimal activity
severity_levels.impact: High risk of heart attack; may require procedures like stenting or bypass

genetic_factors: Family history of early heart disease (before age 55 in men, 65 in women)
environmental_triggers: Unhealthy diet high in saturated fats, trans fats, and sodium
other_causes: Dyslipidemia (high LDL, low HDL, high triglycerides)

primary_symptoms.name: Chest Pain / Angina
primary_symptoms.description: Pressure, tightness, squeezing, or burning sensation in the chest.
primary_symptoms.onset: During exertion, stress, cold weather, or heavy meals

primary_symptoms.name: Shortness of Breath
primary_symptoms.description: Dyspnea, especially on exertion or lying flat.
primary_symptoms.onset: With activity or at rest in advanced cases

primary_symptoms.name: Radiating Pain
primary_symptoms.description: Discomfort spreading to arms (especially left), neck, jaw, shoulders, or back.

secondary_symptoms: Indigestion or heartburn-like symptoms (especially in women)
warning_signs_of_attack: Sudden, severe chest pain not relieved by rest or nitroglycerin
Shortness of breath with sweating or nausea
symptoms_in_children: Extremely rare; usually due to congenital anomalies. May present as chest pain during activity or unexplained fatigue.

medical_history: Personal history of risk factors (smoking, diabetes, hypertension)
physical_examination: Assessment of peripheral pulses and edema

diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detects ischemia, arrhythmias, or prior heart damage
Assesses heart function and wall motion

diagnostic_tests.description: Monitors heart during physical or chemical stress.
Measures cholesterol, cardiac enzymes, and blood sugar.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Assesses risk factors and acute damage

medicines.note: All medications should be taken only under the supervision of a licensed physician. Self-medication can be dangerous.

categories.purpose: Prevent blood clot formation in arteries
Lower LDL cholesterol and stabilize plaques
Reduce heart rate and blood pressure, decreasing oxygen demand
Lower blood pressure and protect heart muscle

diet_and_nutrition.overview: A heart-healthy Mediterranean-style diet significantly reduces progression of CAD by lowering cholesterol, inflammation, and blood pressure.

items.benefit: Omega-3 fatty acids reduce triglycerides and inflammation
Antioxidants and fiber lower blood pressure

sample_meal_plan.note: This is a general guideline. Individual needs vary; consult a dietitian.
sample_meal_plan.early_morning: Warm water + handful of soaked almonds
sample_meal_plan.breakfast: Oatmeal with berries, walnuts, and flaxseeds OR Greek yogurt with fruits
sample_meal_plan.lunch: Grilled fish or lentils + brown rice + large vegetable salad with olive oil
sample_meal_plan.evening_snack: Handful of mixed nuts or carrot sticks with hummus
sample_meal_plan.dinner: Vegetable stir-fry with olive oil + whole grain chapati + grilled chicken or paneer

special_dietary_notes: Limit alcohol to moderate levels if any

trigger_avoidance: Manage stress through meditation or yoga
Avoid extreme cold or heavy physical strain without preparation
Control blood pressure, cholesterol, and diabetes
mental_health: Address anxiety or depression which can worsen outcomes

green_zone.symptoms: No chest pain; normal activity tolerance

yellow_zone.action: Rest, take nitroglycerin if prescribed, contact doctor

red_zone.symptoms: Severe chest pain, shortness of breath, sweating
red_zone.action: MEDICAL EMERGENCY. Take aspirin if advised, call emergency services immediately.

complications.description: Complete blockage leading to heart muscle damage.
Weakened heart muscle unable to pump effectively.

key_points: Pregnancy complications (preeclampsia, gestational diabetes) increase future risk
Careful medication dosing due to kidney function
Rare but serious; requires multidisciplinary care
SCAD (spontaneous coronary artery dissection) more common

vaccinations_recommended.reason: Prevents respiratory infections that strain the heart

when_to_see_doctor: Shortness of breath with minimal activity
emergency_signs: Pain radiating to jaw/arm with sweating/nausea

frequently_asked_questions.question: Is CAD reversible?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Plaque buildup is generally not fully reversible, but progression can be halted or slowed significantly with lifestyle changes and medications.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can I live a normal life with CAD?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes. With proper management, most people with stable CAD lead active, fulfilling lives.

frequently_asked_questions.question: How important is diet in CAD?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Extremely important. A Mediterranean diet combined with exercise is one of the most effective ways to manage the disease.
